# Build a Reusable Alexa+ Pomodoro Routine With Voice Check-Ins

> **In short:** With Alexa+ routines you can chain a 25-minute focus timer, spoken break announcements, a 5-minute break timer, and a back-to-focus message — all from one voice phrase. Alexa+ won't loop forever on its own, so you stop the cycle manually after a few blocks.

A pomodoro is a simple productivity technique (work for a set time, take a short break, repeat) that helps most people beat procrastination and protect deep focus. The Pomodoro Technique, developed by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s, is named after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer he used as a university student. With Alexa+ routines, you can build a reusable cycle that announces each phase out loud and starts the next timer automatically — your hands never leave the keyboard.

## Before you start
- An Alexa+ account. Amazon says Alexa+ is rolling out to invited customers first; open the Alexa app to confirm your device shows the new experience, or check Amazon's Alexa+ page for the latest eligibility details.
- The Alexa app on your phone (free, iOS or Android) and an Echo device — or any Alexa-enabled speaker — signed into the same Amazon account.
- About 10 minutes for the first build, then a few seconds each time you start it. Plan on running one short test cycle (1-minute timers) before trusting it for real work.

## Step 1 — Create a new routine for the focus start
Open the Alexa app, tap the **"⋯" More** tab at the bottom, then choose **"Routines."** Look for a button to create a new routine — in newer app versions it may say **"+ Create routine"** or just a **"+"** in the corner. You'll land on a routine builder screen with two clear sections: **"When this happens"** (the trigger) and **"Add action"** (what Alexa does). Name your routine something you'll remember, like "Start Pomodoro." A *routine* is just a chain of actions Alexa runs automatically when something happens — your trigger phrase, a timer, a schedule, or another routine.
💬 Example: routine name "Start Pomodoro"
You'll know it worked when the routine appears in your routines list with the name you typed.

## Step 2 — Set the voice trigger and the focus announcement
In the **"When this happens"** section, pick the option for a voice phrase — it might be labeled **"Voice," "Say a specific phrase,"** or **"When you say…"** Type the phrase you'll use to start a session, then move down to **"Add action"** and look for **"Alexa Says," "Announce,"** or **"Send Announcement."** Type the message Alexa will read out loud the moment you say your trigger phrase. This is the "hello, focus time" cue that replaces the need to glance at a timer.
💬 Example trigger phrase: "start pomodoro"
💬 Example announcement: "Focus block starting. Twenty-five minutes. I'll let you know when to break."
If it looks different on your device, the trigger list usually lives behind a small **"+"** next to "When this happens." You'll know it worked when the saved routine shows your phrase as the trigger and your message as the first action.

## Step 3 — Add the 25-minute focus timer to the start routine
Still inside "Start Pomodoro," tap **"Add action"** again and look for **"Set Timer"** or **"Wait → Timer."** Set 25 minutes (or your preferred focus length — 20 to 50 minutes is typical) and give the timer a recognizable name like **"Focus."** Naming the timer matters because the next routine will listen for that exact name. The timer begins counting down right after Alexa finishes the opening announcement, so the sequence becomes: announce → start 25-minute timer → wait.
💬 Example: 25-minute timer named exactly "Focus"
If you can't spot a Timer action, scan the "Add action" categories for anything timer- or wait-related. You'll know it worked when the routine shows two actions beneath the voice trigger: your announcement and the Focus timer.

## Step 4 — Build a second routine that fires when the focus timer ends
Go back to the Routines list and create another routine — name it **"Pomodoro Loop."** In **"When this happens,"** pick **"Timer"** (or **"When a timer ends"**) and select the **"Focus"** timer you just created, set to **"Ends."** This is how the chain keeps moving: when the focus timer chimes, this routine wakes up automatically. Add two actions: first, an announcement that break time has started; second, a new timer named **"Break"** set to 5 minutes (or your preferred break length — 3 to 7 minutes is common).
💬 Example announcement: "Break time. Five minutes. Step away from the screen."
💬 Example: 5-minute timer named exactly "Break"
If it looks different, some app versions phrase the trigger as **"When timer named ___ ends"** in plain English. You'll know it worked when the routine list shows "Focus" timer as the trigger for "Pomodoro Loop."

## Step 5 — Add the return-to-focus loop
Now you need a way to restart the focus block when the break timer ends. Two clean approaches, depending on what your app supports. **Approach A:** in the same "Pomodoro Loop" routine, look for an option to add a second **"When this happens"** condition; if it lets you, add **"Break" timer ends** as a second trigger, then add the focus-start announcement plus a fresh 25-minute "Focus" timer. **Approach B (the safer one):** create a third routine called **"Back to Focus,"** trigger it with **"Break" timer ends,** and add the same focus announcement + Focus timer actions. Either way, the cycle becomes: voice → announce + Focus timer → (25 min) → Loop announces break + Break timer → (5 min) → Back to Focus announces + Focus timer → repeat.
💬 Example announcement: "Back to focus. Twenty-five minutes starting now."
💬 Example: 25-minute timer named "Focus" again
If it looks different, older app versions may only allow one trigger per routine — use Approach B in that case. You'll know it worked when both "Focus" and "Break" appear as timer names somewhere across your routines, and the list shows two or three routines connected by those names.

## Step 6 — Save and run one quick test cycle
Tap **"Save"** (usually a checkmark or button in the top-right corner) on every routine. Stand near your Echo and say **"Alexa, start pomodoro"** — or whatever phrase you set. You should hear the focus announcement, then a 25-minute countdown. For the first test, temporarily set both timers to 1 minute so you can confirm the loop end-to-end without waiting. Listen for the "Break time" announcement exactly when the first timer chimes, then the "Back to focus" announcement when the second timer ends. If a routine doesn't fire, the cause is almost always a spelling mismatch — "Focus" in one routine and "focus timer" in another counts as two different names.
💬 Example test: change both timers to 1 minute the first time, then change them back to 25 and 5 once the chain is proven
You'll know it worked when each phase begins the moment the previous timer ends, with no further input from you.

## Step 7 — Use it in a real session and know how to stop it
Say your trigger phrase at the start of your work block and ignore your phone. After each focus block you'll hear "Break time" and a short countdown begins; after each break you'll hear "Back to focus" and a new focus timer starts. The cycle repeats until you cancel it. A simple **"Alexa, stop"** ends the current timer and breaks the chain — no further announcements will follow. Honest limitation: Alexa+ won't recognize that you're "done for the day" on its own, so you'll repeat the loop as long as it helps, then stop it manually. If the spoken cues are too loud for a shared space, lower the Echo volume or set a **Do Not Disturb** schedule in the Alexa app so announcements don't disturb others.
💬 Example stop command: "Alexa, stop"
You'll know it worked when your Echo goes silent and no new timer fires after you say stop.

## Common mistakes
- **Mismatched timer names.** The loop breaks silently if "Focus" in routine A is "focus" or "Focus timer" in routine B. Use identical capitalization and spacing in every routine — treat the name like a password.
- **Assuming one routine can have two triggers.** Some Alexa app versions only allow one "When this happens" condition per routine. If your multi-trigger setup silently does nothing, fall back to Approach B in Step 5: create a third routine for the return-to-focus phase.
- **Skipping the break.** It's tempting to chain only focus timers for "more deep work," but the break is what makes the technique work — your brain needs the reset. Keep a real break, even if you shorten it.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** The spoken announcement removes the "is it time yet?" glance that breaks concentration. You can leave your phone in another room and still know exactly where you are in the cycle, because Alexa tells you.
- **For your work or work-from-home setup:** Run the routine during deep-work hours and pair it with a single calendar entry — "Deep work, no meetings" — so colleagues can see when you're heads-down. The routine handles the timing; the calendar handles the interruptions.
- **If you want to go further:** Add a **"Music"** action to the focus phase that plays a focus-friendly playlist (lo-fi, rain sounds, white noise) and add a **"Pause music"** or **"Set volume to 0"** action to the break phase. The same routine builder accepts both — and you'll have an audio cue layer on top of the spoken one.

## Try it now
Open the Alexa app, tap **Routines**, and create one routine named **"Start Pomodoro"** with a single 1-minute timer named **"Focus."** Say **"Alexa, start pomodoro"** once. When the timer ends, you've proven the basic chain — every other step in this guide is just adding the next link.
